message: Hi Ana, thanks for joining. I'll be interviewing you for the Backend Engineer role at Northwind Freight. We have about 12 minutes. To start, tell me briefly about your background and what drew you to this role.

Sure. I've spent the last four years on the orders platform at a logistics company, writing Node.js services in TypeScript on top of PostgreSQL. What drew me to this role is that tracking shipments is the same shape of problem, lots of state changes that have to be exactly right, and I like that you run your own clusters.
You mention clusters. Walk me through a time you deployed or operated a service on Kubernetes yourself.

Last year we moved the six orders services from a hand-built VM setup to a managed Kubernetes cluster. I owned that migration. I wrote the Helm charts for all six services, set resource requests and limits by looking at a month of metrics, and did the rollout one service at a time behind the load balancer. The part I got wrong at first was readiness probes, the first service flapped because the probe hit an endpoint that needed the database. After I fixed that the rollout of the other five went without a page, and our deploy time went from forty minutes to about six.
Good. Have you been part of an on-call rotation? Tell me about an incident you handled.

Yes, I was in a weekly rotation of five engineers for about two years. The incident I remember best was a Saturday when order confirmations stopped going out. The alert was a queue depth alarm. I found that the confirmation service had exhausted its PostgreSQL connection pool because a new feature opened a connection per request and never released it on the error path. I rolled back the deploy first to stop the bleeding, then wrote the fix on Monday with a test that counts open connections, and I added a pool saturation alert so we'd see it before the queue backed up next time. I also wrote the postmortem.
What did the postmortem change about how the team worked?

Two things. We added a checklist item for anything touching the database layer, does it release on every path, and we started running the connection count test in CI. It sounds small but we didn't have that class of incident again while I was there.
The posting lists GraphQL as a plus. What's your experience designing a GraphQL API?

I built a GraphQL gateway for our mobile team. They were making six REST calls to render the order screen, so I put a GraphQL layer in front of the existing services. The design decision I'd call out is that I kept mutations thin, each one maps to exactly one existing REST endpoint, because I didn't want the gateway to own business logic. For queries I used DataLoader to batch the per-order lookups, which took the order screen from six round trips to one. The mobile team's screen load went from about two seconds to under half a second on a slow connection.
Tell me about a PostgreSQL query you tuned and how you found it.

The nightly reporting job was taking forty minutes and growing. I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the main query and found a sequential scan on the orders table joined to shipments. Adding a composite index on customer id and created date, and rewriting one correlated subquery as a join, took it to nine minutes. I verified it on a copy of production data first because the index was large.
Last one. Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision on your team and what you did.

When we planned the Kubernetes migration, the lead wanted to move all six services in one weekend. I pushed back because we had no experience with the cluster yet. I proposed one service per week starting with the least critical one, and I wrote up the risk of each service so the order was based on something. He agreed, and honestly the readiness probe problem I mentioned would have taken down everything if we'd done it in one go.
That's a good place to stop. Thank you, Ana. Your feedback will follow shortly.
